summary: Describes version 2.0 of Certificate Transparency, a system for publicly logging TLS server certificates so anyone can audit certificate authority activity and spot suspect certificates. The intent is that clients would eventually refuse certificates that are not logged. It is experimental and obsoletes RFC 6962.

plainLanguage.summary: Certificate Transparency records public TLS certificates in logs that can be checked by anyone. The logs do not stop an incorrect certificate from being issued, but they can make it easier to detect.

questions: what is a signed certificate timestamp
what is a merkle tree inclusion proof
subtitle: Append-only public logs let anyone check whether TLS certificates have been recorded.

tldr.problem: A certification authority can issue a certificate that a domain owner did not expect, and the owner may not otherwise learn about it.
tldr.mechanism: Logs record certificates in append-only Merkle Trees, issue signed timestamps as promises to include entries, and provide proofs for monitoring and auditing.
tldr.outcome: The logs help detect misissuance but do not prevent it. RFC 9162 is Experimental and obsoletes RFC 6962.

today: RFC 9162 is an Experimental RFC published in December 2021. It obsoletes RFC 6962, and the batch metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Certificate Transparency Does
sections.content:
Certificate Transparency (CT) aims to help detect misissued public TLS server certificates by recording them in append-only logs. Anyone can submit a certificate chain, and a log returns a Signed Certificate Timestamp (SCT) when it accepts a submission.

Certificate owners and others can monitor logs for unexpected certificates. Checking whether entries are included is asynchronous, so a TLS client can continue without waiting for that check to finish.
sections.plainLanguage: A log gives a signed promise to record a submitted certificate. People responsible for a domain can check the public records for certificates they did not expect.

sections.title: Merkle Trees and Proofs
sections.content:
Each log is a binary Merkle Tree. A leaf hash uses a 0x00 prefix before its data, and an interior-node hash uses a 0x01 prefix before its children; the different prefixes separate the two kinds of input.

An inclusion proof supplies the other tree nodes needed to calculate the root from a particular leaf. A consistency proof shows that an older tree is a prefix of a newer tree, supporting the append-only property.
sections.plainLanguage: A log summarizes its entries in a tree of hashes. Proofs let a client check that an entry is present and that a newer tree preserves the older entries.

sections.title: Entries, Timestamps, and Tree Heads
sections.content:
A submission can be a certificate or a precertificate, which is a CA-signed object created before the corresponding certificate is issued. A precertificate's signature represents the CA's intent to issue that certificate.

An SCT is the log's signed promise to add an accepted submission to its tree within the Maximum Merge Delay (MMD). A Signed Tree Head (STH) records a timestamp, tree size, and root hash, and the log signs it.
sections.plainLanguage: The SCT is a signed promise that a log will add a certificate entry. A signed tree head records the current size and hash of the log.

sections.title: Log Queries and TLS Delivery
sections.content:
Clients communicate with logs using HTTPS GET and POST messages, with JSON responses and base64-encoded binary data. They can submit entries, retrieve tree heads, request inclusion or consistency proofs, fetch entries, and obtain accepted trust anchors.

TLS servers can present SCTs through a TLS extension, a stapled OCSP response, or a certificate extension. CT-using clients must support all three methods, validate SCTs, and apply local policy when deciding whether the presented evidence is sufficient.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients can submit certificates and ask logs for signed tree information or proofs. Servers can send SCTs to clients in several ways during a TLS handshake.

sections.title: What Logs Can and Cannot Guarantee
sections.content:
An SCT proves that a log promised to publish a certificate, but it does not guarantee that monitors have noticed a problem or that a certificate will be revoked. Logs may also misbehave by missing deadlines or showing different views to different clients.

Detecting inconsistent views requires clients to compare signed tree heads, a technique called gossip that this RFC does not define. Fetching inclusion proofs directly from a log can reveal which TLS server a client contacted, so servers are encouraged to provide proofs.
sections.plainLanguage: CT makes certificates easier to inspect, but it does not itself stop misissuance or guarantee that someone will act on a warning. Logs still need monitoring and auditing.
